description: Our team is developing the 'Mars Survival Handbook' for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge!!!
summary: The project develops an educational web platform named "Mars Survival Handbook," providing a comprehensive knowledge system on the journey of Mars colonization through 5 core modules: Discover Mars, Survival Knowledge, Living on Mars, Science & Technology, and Human Survival. The website addresses the lack of intuitive, accurate, and accessible global space science resources. It serves as a vital tool for students, future explorers, and the international science-enthusiastic community to access precise data directly from NASA, thereby sparking creative thinking and shaping humanity's future beyond Earth.
details:
Mars Survival Handbook is an interactive web app that lets students plan a simulated expedition on Mars. We built it around a decision an exploration crew might face at Jezero Crater. The ancient river delta is close enough to visit, but does the crew have time to stop there, study the rocks, and return to its habitat with a safety reserve? The user chooses where to go and how much time to spend on science. The app shows what those choices would cost in time and oxygen.
Planning starts on a map with two views from NASA’s Mars Trek. The Viking image mosaic shows surface features, while elevation data from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) lets users see how the terrain rises and falls. Users can explore sites such as Perseverance’s landing area at Jezero Crater or Curiosity’s at Gale Crater. Short descriptions explain why each location matters. After choosing a site, the user places a habitat, draws a route by adding waypoints, and sees which scientific targets lie near the path.
The planner measures the distance between waypoints using Mars’s radius of 3,389.5 km. If the crew will return along the same path, it counts both legs. It then uses the selected walking speed to calculate travel time, adds time for science stops, and estimates oxygen use from the total duration. GO means the crew can complete the route with its chosen reserve intact. CAUTION means the crew would use part of that reserve. NO-GO means the route would take longer than the suit can support. For example, with an eight-hour suit and a 25% reserve, the crew has six hours available before it starts using that reserve. A proposed stop that extends a trip from five hours and 45 minutes to six hours and 15 minutes changes the result from GO to CAUTION. The student can then shorten the route, drop the stop, or choose a closer target and see how the result changes.
We built the application in C# with Blazor, used JavaScript and Leaflet for the interactive map, and developed an ASP.NET Core API backed by Azure SQL for the handbook content. One design decision was to make the origin of the information clear. NASA supplies the imagery, elevation data, and mission context. Walking speed, suit duration, and the safety reserve are visible assumptions that users can adjust. We also included a coordinate grid so users can continue drawing routes if NASA’s map imagery is unavailable.
Our goal is to give teachers and students a practical exercise in scientific decision-making. Two groups can start from the same habitat and propose different expeditions. One might spend longer at a nearby geological site, while the other might walk farther and make fewer stops. Each group can use its map, time estimate, and remaining reserve to explain what it hopes to learn and why its crew should make the trip.
